title: US Congress Calls Trump's Russian Diesel Deal Illegal as 'Energy Ceasefire' Lands
subhead: Seven senators say the 300,000-tonne Russian diesel arrangement violates US law, while Trump claims Russia and Ukraine have agreed to stop hitting energy infrastructure. Oil slipped on the news even as Houthi strikes on Riyadh and a tanker hit near Oman keep supply risk live.

sections.heading: The Russian diesel deal hits a legal wall
sections.body:
Trump's plan to import Russian diesel is running into open congressional opposition. On Sunday a bipartisan group of seven US senators — four Republicans (Susan Collins, Lisa Murkowski, Thom Tillis, John Curtis) and three Democrats (Jeanne Shaheen, Richard Blumenthal, Ron Wyden) — said the deal violated US law and urged the president to 'reverse course', according to BBC News. Congress 'explicitly banned Russian energy imports in 2022', the lawmakers argued, and the US 'should not provide Putin with a financial lifeline while Russia continues to kill Ukrainian civilians'.

The substance of the deal, announced Friday: Putin agreed to release 300,000 tonnes of diesel immediately, then 500,000 tonnes in November, one million more after that, and a further three million 'within a short period', per Trump's Truth Social post. Russia's Deputy PM Alexander Novak confirmed the volumes to TASS, saying exports could reach three million tonnes per month in future. The US Treasury is suspending sanctions on Russian diesel exports until 7 April, though other Russian assets in US banks remain frozen.

The trigger is domestic politics as much as supply. BBC reports the average US diesel price is $6.28 a gallon, down from a record $6.53 in late September, with farm states hit hardest ahead of next month's midterms. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent dismissed the legal objections on Fox News, saying the arrangement 'would work through existing legal channels'. Analysts quoted by the BBC questioned whether Russia can physically deliver those volumes — the US burns about 3.6 million barrels of diesel a day, so the initial 300,000 tonnes is roughly half a day's consumption spread over a month.
sections.whyItMatters: Washington is now openly importing the fuel it has spent two years telling India and Europe not to buy. Even if the volumes are modest, the precedent — and the bipartisan legal fight — will define how enforceable US energy sanctions look to every other buyer.

sections.heading: An 'energy ceasefire' that only one side confirms
sections.body:
Trump announced Sunday that Russia and Ukraine had reached an 'energy ceasefire', effective immediately, but gave no details (BBC, AP). Ukraine's Zelenskyy welcomed the idea but said he was unaware of any such agreement being concluded, and noted that if Moscow agreed, Kyiv would accept. There has been no confirmation from Moscow.

Politico and Yahoo report the scope appears to be narrow — likely limited to oil refineries and energy infrastructure rather than a broader truce. That matters because Ukraine's drone campaign against Russian refineries has been the single biggest brake on Russia's ability to export refined products, including the diesel now headed to the US. AP reported a Ukrainian drone strike shut down a data centre run by Russian tech giant Yandex on Sunday.

Zelenskyy had offered to halt refinery strikes only if Moscow stopped hitting Ukraine's energy infrastructure. With no Russian response, the 'ceasefire' remains a US claim rather than a verified arrangement.
sections.whyItMatters: If it holds, a refinery truce would free up Russian refining capacity exactly as the diesel deal needs it. If it doesn't, the diesel promise rests on refineries Ukraine is still targeting — making the supply boost fragile from day one.

sections.heading: Oil slips on ceasefire hopes while the Gulf stays hot
sections.body:
Crude fell Monday as traders priced in the prospect of more Russian supply. Reuters reported Brent had ended last week at $104.72 and WTI at $91.85 (Al Attiyah Foundation's 10 October review), before slipping toward $90 a barrel in Asian trade on Monday (FXStreet). TD Securities noted that $90 is proving a pivotal level for trend-following CTAs, with positioning whipsawing around it.

The de-escalation signal is not matched by events on the ground. Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport was struck again on Sunday by Houthi militants, a day after an attack killed 12 people and injured more than 300 (FXStreet). A drone also hit an oil tanker near the Sohar anchorage off Oman, just outside the Strait of Hormuz, over the weekend. Trump said he would 'look at' joining Saudi Arabia's fight against the Houthis.

Separately, the US Department of Energy approved an emergency exchange of up to 4 million barrels of crude from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve to offset disruptions from Hurricane Isaias, which shut in roughly 1.3 million barrels per day — about 70% of US Gulf output (Al Attiyah Foundation).
sections.whyItMatters: Two opposing forces are setting the price: Russian supply returning versus a Gulf security environment that keeps producing new attacks. The $90 level has become the market's line in the sand, and it is being tested in both directions.

sections.heading: Iran stalls Hormuz talks, offers itself as Houthi–Saudi broker
sections.body:
Iran's security chief Mohsen Rezaei said Washington's response to Tehran's seven conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz was 'insufficient' (Reuters, via IRJ and Moneycontrol), claiming the US accepted only some of the conditions. Tehran wants the remaining issues clarified before indirect talks resume — with nuclear negotiations still explicitly off the table.

In a parallel move, Iran's foreign minister urged diplomacy in a call with his Saudi counterpart and offered to facilitate talks between Saudi Arabia and Yemen's Houthis following the deadly strikes on the kingdom (MSN/Al Jazeera). Meanwhile Reuters reported that tanker traffic through Hormuz has recovered to about 81% of pre-war levels, even as attacks rise.

The New York Times assessed that Saudi Arabia 'has few options' as the Houthis hit the heart of its economic ambitions, describing the conflict as deeply asymmetrical. Gulf states, per Al Attiyah data, still hold gas storage at just 73.12% — the lowest for this time of year since records began in 2011.
sections.whyItMatters: Iran is simultaneously holding Hormuz hostage and offering to be the region's peacemaker. That dual posture suggests Tehran wants to convert its remaining chokepoint leverage into diplomatic relevance before the war's economic pressure erodes it.

sections.heading: The rare-earth clock nobody is watching
sections.body:
A one-year suspension of China's toughest rare-earth export rules expires on 10 November — five weeks away — with no sign of renewal. Beijing's Ministry of Commerce agreed the pause on 7 November 2025, freezing an October 2025 regime that included extraterritorial licensing over foreign-made products containing even trace Chinese-origin rare earths (Startup Fortune, citing Mining Technology data).

The underlying controls were never lifted: case-by-case licences still apply to seven medium and heavy rare earths — samarium, gadolinium, terbium, dysprosium, lutetium, scandium and yttrium. China produced about 270,000 tonnes of the ~390,000 tonnes of global rare-earth oxide in 2025 (69.2%), and processes up to 90% of the world's rare earths — near 99% for the heaviest elements. The IEA has warned that full implementation could threaten $6.5 trillion of downstream production outside China, with automotive alone accounting for over $3 trillion.

Beijing has explicitly linked rare-earth magnet approvals to US restrictions on advanced AI chip exports, making the 10 November decision a bargaining chip in a wider tech negotiation.
sections.whyItMatters: Unlike an oil spike, a rare-earth cutoff would hit EV motors, wind turbines, chips and defence hardware simultaneously. The deadline is fixed, unresolved and weeks away — a slow-burn risk that is getting less attention than it deserves.

sections.heading: World Bank preps crisis aid as energy shock spreads to the Global South
sections.body:
The World Bank is in talks with 30 to 40 countries about crisis aid to manage energy price increases triggered by the Middle East war, president Ajay Banga said in Bangkok, ahead of the IMF–World Bank meetings (Reuters/Economic Times). Banga said more countries were asking to retool existing projects than to draw on the immediate crisis window, and that the Bank could deploy as much as $100 billion if conditions worsen — more than the $70 billion disbursed during the pandemic.

Separately in Africa, Nigerian billionaire Aliko Dangote's $16 billion, 700,000-barrel-per-day Lamu refinery in Kenya is facing mounting disclosure pressure less than two weeks after groundbreaking. Kenya's The Star editorialised on 11 October that the deal 'must be placed under the microscope', and a Nairobi High Court certified an urgent petition on 6 October seeking disclosure of public money, land and tax incentives (Billionaires.Africa). Kenya has considered taking 10% for about $500 million. Dangote's Lagos refinery IPO closes on 13 October, with Nigeria's finance minister saying on 9 October the country lacks enough crude to fully supply that plant.
sections.whyItMatters: The war's energy shock is now an IMF-World Bank agenda item affecting dozens of developing economies, while large African refining bets are being built on contested terms. The financial plumbing of the crisis is spreading well beyond the Gulf.

bottomLine: Washington moved from sanctioning Russian energy to buying it, and immediately ran into a bipartisan legal challenge — with seven senators calling the diesel deal unlawful and Trump claiming an unconfirmed 'energy ceasefire' to make it work. Oil slipped toward $90 on the prospect of returning Russian supply, but the Gulf kept generating fresh risk: another Houthi strike on Riyadh's airport, a tanker hit near Oman, and Iran still refusing to reopen Hormuz on US terms. The quieter stories may matter more over time — a rare-earth export deadline five weeks out with $6.5 trillion of IEA-flagged exposure, and a World Bank already talking crisis aid with 30-40 countries. The near-term market is being pulled by two forces that cancel each other out; the structural risks are building underneath.
sources: BBC News, Reuters, AP, Politico, FXStreet, Al Attiyah Foundation (Marhaba Qatar), Moneycontrol, IRJ, MSN/Al Jazeera, New York Times, Startup Fortune/Mining Technology, IEA, Economic Times, Billionaires.Africa, TASS, Truth Social
